title: A small system, end to end
summary: Deploy an event-driven product-manual assistant. Follow uploads, indexing, questions and answers through the whole system.
text:
The outcome:  upload a fictional product manual, wait for indexing, and ask a question whose answer includes the actual supporting passages. You receive all application code. Your work is to understand, configure, deploy and inspect it.  
   You will learn:  how a small RAG system fits together, which component owns each state transition, and how to follow this self-paced path.   Starting requirements:  experience writing software. Azure, Python, Docker, Kubernetes and RAG can be new to you. The next chapter checks your environment before anything paid is created.   Working context:  read here; all later commands run in Bash from the repository root, the folder containing the site's  index.html .  
 Before you start 
 Prepare an  Azure account with an active subscription , permission to create resources and assign roles, and quota/access for the chosen VM and models. Locally you need  Azure CLI, Bicep, Docker, kubectl, Java 21, Python 3.12+, Git and the supporting Bash tools . Windows participants use  Ubuntu 24.04 in WSL2 with Docker Desktop integration . You create your own AKS cluster during the workshop. 
 Use the  full pre-workshop checklist  and  downloadable Windows/Ubuntu setup scripts  before beginning the four-hour core path. Installation, restarts and account/quota approvals are preparation time. Terms throughout the workshop use the site's dotted-underlined tooltips; the  shared jargon page  contains all definitions and sources. 
 What you will deploy 
  Products  is a Java 21 / Spring Boot application on AKS. It has two views: upload a product and chat about products. Thymeleaf renders the pages; a little browser JavaScript polls for status. JDBC and explicit SQL persist products, questions and answers. There is no ORM or separate SPA. 
  ProductsEmbedder  is a small Python Azure Function. A Blob Storage notification starts it. It turns UTF-8 manual text into chunks and embeddings and stores them in PostgreSQL with pgvector. 
  ProductsChat  is a Python container on AKS. It receives questions from Service Bus, retrieves relevant chunks, calls an Azure-hosted chat model and publishes a reply. KEDA changes its replica count. Products keeps at least one replica running. 
 The upload and embedding flow 
   Browser → Products Commit product + immutable manual ID  →   Private blob Upload the .txt file  →   Event Grid → Function BlobCreated notification; read and chunk  →   Embedding model → PostgreSQL 1536-value vectors + text; mark ready  The database record commits before the blob is uploaded. The Function can therefore resolve the product even if the event arrives immediately.  
 Blob Storage organizes objects as  containers  containing  blobs . A storage container is not a Docker container. Event Grid carries a notification that something happened; the notification does not contain the manual itself. The Blob trigger's extension fetches it using the Function's managed identity. 
 The question and answer flow 
   Products + PostgreSQL Persist request + outbox; return request ID  →   Service Bus request queue Buffer queued work  →   ProductsChat Embed question → retrieve → generate  →   Reply queue → Products Persist answer + sources; browser polls  Every message includes a request ID and correlation ID. Nothing depends on one HTTP request or browser tab staying open.  
 Embeddings support retrieval: related text should be nearby in vector space. They do not write the answer. The LLM generates an answer from the question and the retrieved reference text. The reference text is untrusted data, never an instruction to override the application prompt. 
 The four-hour boundary 
 The ten core chapters total an  estimated 240 minutes , once tools and Azure access are ready. Start long provisioning early and read/build while it runs. Model-access approvals, quota increases, large downloads and unusual provisioning delays are outside that estimate. This duration has not been established by a timed participant walkthrough. 
 This is selected AI-200 practice, not complete exam preparation. You exercise ACR, AKS manifests, PostgreSQL/vector retrieval, Service Bus, Event Grid, Functions, Key Vault and App Configuration. The exam specifically places one KEDA objective under  Container Apps ; our AKS KEDA exercise teaches the mechanism without claiming to cover Container Apps revisions. See the  concise objective mapping . 
  Optional depth: deliberately outside the core path  Production SSO, public CA certificates, a custom domain, private endpoints for every Azure service, independent database roles, manual replacement/deletion, ANN index tuning and distributed tracing are extensions. The core uses one small database owner, one AKS node and an IP-restricted, self-signed HTTPS endpoint. These choices are documented rather than presented as production defaults.  
 Check your understanding 
  Verification:  locate the three application directories in the  source explorer . Explain why upload success is different from a manual being ready, and why Event Grid and Service Bus both appear. Then continue to the prerequisite checker. 
 Common starting mistakes    Expecting the documentation to provision Azure:  this website is static and needs no Azure credentials. Only explicitly executed scripts create cloud resources.   Starting with an existing cluster:  none is required. The supplied stages create a separate workshop AKS cluster and isolate its kubeconfig.   Using real product documents:  use the three fictional manuals provided. The application calls a paid Azure model and is not a production data-handling platform.

title: Check your starting point
summary: Use one Bash environment and catch permissions, quota and model-access blockers early.
text:
You will learn:  how to make Azure identity, regional availability and quota explicit before starting expensive work.   Starting requirements:  a suitable Azure subscription and permission to create resources and role assignments. Software installation is preparation time, not part of the four-hour estimate.   Shell and directory:  Bash, at the repository root. On Windows use Ubuntu 24.04 in WSL2, with Docker Desktop's WSL integration enabled for that distribution. Keep this environment for every Azure command.  
 Have these ready before the workshop 
   Azure account and subscription:  a Microsoft or work/school account that can sign in to an active Azure subscription. An account alone is not a subscription. Confirm billing or credits cover the selected services, accept the  estimated costs , and choose a development subscription you can clean up afterward. A free/trial subscription does not guarantee the required model or VM quota.   Azure permissions:  Owner, or Contributor plus Role Based Access Control Administrator, at subscription scope. Arrange this with the subscription owner before starting. You need to create resources, register providers and assign identities; tenant administration alone does not grant these permissions.   Capacity and model access:  the chosen region must support AKS, PostgreSQL, Functions Flex and the selected chat/embedding models. The checker below verifies offers and quotas; the next chapter makes real model calls before starting AKS. Resolve organizational restrictions and quota requests in advance.   A development computer:  a browser, the supplied repository files and a terminal. For the supplied Windows installer use supported x64 Windows 11 with hardware virtualization enabled and local administrator access. We recommend 16 GB RAM and 30 GB free disk space for WSL, images and build caches. Follow  Docker's current system requirements  if using another supported Windows configuration.   Network access:  allow software/package downloads, Azure sign-in and Azure service endpoints. Know whether a corporate proxy, VPN or device policy blocks Docker/WSL, package installation or cloud resource creation.   Local software:  the tools listed below, installed in the same Bash environment, and a running Linux-container Docker engine. No pre-existing AKS cluster, database or other Azure resources are required.  
 Windows: download the setup script 
  Yes, the documented Windows path uses Docker Desktop.  It provides the local Linux-container engine for building, running, tagging and pushing images. Start it during the workshop. On native Linux an existing Docker Engine 24+ with BuildKit is sufficient. Merely reading or serving this documentation does not require Docker or Azure access. 
  Download Windows setup (.ps1)  ·  Download Ubuntu tool setup (.sh) . Review   scripts/setup-windows.ps1   and   scripts/setup-ubuntu.sh   before running them. They install local software only and do not sign in, register Azure providers or create cloud resources. Review  Docker Desktop's license terms  for your organization. The WinGet invocation accepts package/source agreements; application first-run setup remains interactive. 
  Open  PowerShell as Administrator , change to the folder containing the downloaded  setup-windows.ps1  (normally Downloads), and run the command below. Add  -WhatIf  to preview the actions. The process-only execution-policy flag permits this reviewed script without changing the machine's saved execution policy. If WinGet is missing, install/update Microsoft's  App Installer  first.  
   PowerShell · Windows Downloads folder  Copy    powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\setup-windows.ps1
    Canonical commands:   scripts/setup-windows.ps1   
  The script uses  WinGet  to install Docker Desktop and  wsl --install --distribution Ubuntu-24.04 --no-launch  to enable/install WSL and Ubuntu. Existing installations are preserved. Restart if Windows requests it, then rerun the script to finish. Allow download/restart time before the four-hour core path.  Open Ubuntu 24.04 from Start, or run  wsl -d Ubuntu-24.04 . Create a Linux username/password on first launch. In PowerShell,  wsl --list --verbose  must show version  2  for this distribution.  Start Docker Desktop. Select the  WSL2 engine  and  Linux containers ; under  Settings → Resources → WSL Integration , enable  Ubuntu-24.04  and apply the change. A local Kubernetes cluster in Docker Desktop is unnecessary.  In  Ubuntu Bash , copy/extract the supplied repository into a Linux folder such as  ~/ai200 , then open that repository root. You should see  index.html  and  workshop/ . A Windows checkout can also be reached through  /mnt/c/ , although a Linux filesystem copy avoids slower bind mounts and line-ending issues. Run the supplied Ubuntu setup from the repository, so it can also install the workshop's Python requirements:  
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/setup-ubuntu.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The Ubuntu script uses apt for Java 21, Python 3.12, Bash, Git, jq, curl, OpenSSL, archive tools and Azure CLI from Microsoft's signed repository. It installs Bicep 0.49.2 and checksum-verifies kubectl 1.34.1. It creates  workshop/.tools/venv  for the pinned client dependencies. It does not install a second Docker daemon inside WSL. Windows Azure CLI, Python and Java installations do not substitute for these Linux tools. 
 Have the tools already? Skip installation and run this local check, which requires neither Azure sign-in nor bootstrap state: 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    python3 workshop/tools/preflight.py --local-only
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 Prepare one environment 
 Install  WSL2  and enable  Docker Desktop integration  if you use Windows. Run the commands inside Ubuntu, not a PowerShell tab. macOS and Linux Bash also work if the listed tools are available. Images target  linux/amd64 , matching the supplied AKS node. 
    Tool  Required role/version  Check in Bash      Python + venv/pip  3.12+ for local tooling; deployed Python is 3.12   python3 --version     Java  21 LTS; Maven 3.9.11 is supplied by Wrapper and Docker   java -version     Azure CLI + Bicep  CLI 2.91+; installer pins Bicep 0.49.2   az version ,  az bicep version     Docker  A running Linux-container engine 24+ with BuildKit; Docker Desktop + WSL2 integration on Windows   docker info     kubectl  1.32+; installer uses 1.34.1. Stay within one minor of the deployed AKS version; adjust the client after checking  kubectl version  if needed.   kubectl version --client     Other commands  Bash 4+, Git, jq 1.6+, curl, OpenSSL 3, zip/unzip  The checker tests their presence    
 Use Microsoft's  Azure CLI installation instructions  and  az bicep install . Use  az aks install-cli  if you need kubectl. Helm, a local Functions host and a local PostgreSQL installation are not required for the core path: Azure CLI handles Function package deployment; AKS supplies KEDA. 
 Sign in with  az login , select the intended subscription using  az account set --subscription ... , then inspect  az account show . This is the one subscription choice to make deliberately. Do not continue if the selected subscription belongs to a customer or production environment. 
 Create the small bootstrap configuration 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    python3 workshop/tools/bootstrap.py
bash workshop/scripts/00-check.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The bootstrap tool reads the selected subscription, chooses  swedencentral , and creates names from the prefix  raglab  plus a subscription-derived suffix. It detects the calling network's public IPv4 and restricts the Products service to that  /32 . Review the printed non-secret configuration. 
 Use  --subscription ,  --location ,  --prefix  or  --allowed-cidr  on   tools/bootstrap.py   when needed, or provide a reviewed copy of   config.example.json   with  --config . The prefix must contain 3–8 lowercase letters/digits and start with a letter; generated Storage, ACR and Key Vault names respect their length/character constraints. Globally unique names may still be reserved or soft-deleted: change the prefix before creating resources if Azure reports a collision. 
  workshop/.state/config.json  contains non-secret resume state and is ignored by Git. Scripts reuse it rather than silently switching subscriptions. Do not edit its subscription or prefix after creating resources. The website never reads it and never asks you to put credentials in browser storage or URLs. 
 If several participants share one Azure subscription, give each person a distinct prefix before provisioning. The default prefix intentionally reuses the same workshop resources in that subscription; it is not per-browser isolation. 
 Read and fix the checker results 
   tools/preflight.py   checks tool versions, Docker, sign-in, subscription state, provider registration, creation/role-assignment permissions, regional service offers, a compatible VM SKU, CPU quota including upgrade surge, and model offers/quota. It stops on unknown critical quota results; a missing API response is not evidence of capacity. 
 Use  Owner , or  Contributor plus Role Based Access Control Administrator , at subscription scope for this workshop. A resource-scoped Contributor alone cannot register providers or assign the required identities. Organizational policy and deny assignments can still block operations even when these roles are present. 
 If providers are unregistered, the following explicitly registers them, waits with a bounded readiness check, and reruns the checks. Unregistered Compute or model providers can also make quota/offer queries return empty results, so register first rather than assuming that empty results prove no quota: 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/00-check.sh --register
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
   Expensive blockers:  one D4ds_v5 node needs four vCPUs, and the check reserves another four for an upgrade surge. Confirm PostgreSQL Burstable capacity and Flex regional quota in the portal if your subscription restricts them. Model listings are not proof of inference access; chapter 3 creates only the model resource first and makes actual calls before AKS starts.  
 Prepare the small verification environment 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    python3 -m venv workshop/.tools/venv
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source workshop/.tools/venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r workshop/requirements-test.txt
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 This virtual environment is for smoke/load tools and local tests. It does not change the Python installed by Azure Functions. To resume in another terminal, run  source workshop/.tools/venv/bin/activate . Container builds install their own pinned requirements. 
 Expected results and common failures 
  Verification:  the checker should end with “All read-only gates passed.” This is expected output, not a claim about your subscription. At this point no paid resources should have been created. 
   Docker daemon unavailable:  start Docker Desktop, enable this WSL distribution, reopen Ubuntu and retry  docker info .   Java version is not 21:  install OpenJDK 21 and set  JAVA_HOME  and  PATH  in this Bash session. A Windows JDK outside WSL does not install a Linux JDK.   Quota/API response missing:  use Azure portal → Subscription → Usage + quotas. Ask the owner to increase the chosen VM family and model quota, or choose a region offering all required services. Do not bypass the check by reducing it to zero.   Role assignment write denied:  ask the subscription owner for the role stated above. Tenant admin consent is different from Azure resource RBAC.   Your public IP changes:  stop and update the allowed  /32  before applying the service. A VPN can change which address Azure sees.  
  Continue when:  all read-only checks pass, the subscription is correct and the cost explanation in the next chapter is acceptable.

title: Start the Azure resources
summary: Prove model access, create the shared network, then start AKS and PostgreSQL while you work on Docker.
text:
You will learn:  how to provision dependent Azure resources in understandable stages and prove model access before starting a cluster.   Starting requirements:  the prerequisite checker passes; the selected subscription, region and source IP are correct.   Shell and directory:  Bash, repository root. Keep the virtual environment available for later verification tools.  
 Read the cost boundary first 
 This is a  paid workshop . A planning estimate checked on  11 November 2026  is roughly  US$5–15 for one four-hour walkthrough  with the small sample and prompt cleanup, before tax, discounts and subscription-specific rates. This is an allowance, not a measured bill or a guaranteed price. Resources left running for a day can cost materially more. 
 Main drivers are the AKS VM and disk, PostgreSQL compute/storage, NAT gateway and public IPs, Standard Service Bus/App Configuration, model tokens, and any diagnostic ingestion. AKS's Free management tier does not make its VM free. GlobalStandard model processing may occur outside the account's region. Check the  Azure calculator  and your subscription's actual offers; the  reference page lists cost drivers . You will deliberately confirm the group name before the first creation. 
 Start the first two stages 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/01-models.sh
bash workshop/scripts/02-provision.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 Stage 01: models before machines 
   scripts/01-models.sh   checks prerequisites again, creates a tagged workshop-only resource group, and deploys   infra/models.bicep  . It creates an Azure OpenAI resource with key authentication disabled, a chat deployment named  chat , and an embedding deployment named  embedding . Versions, SKUs and requested capacities come from the bootstrap configuration. 
 The default chat model is  gpt-5-mini , version  2025-08-07 ; the embedding model is  text-embedding-3-small , version  1 .   tools/model_probe.py   obtains an Entra token, requests one 1536-dimensional embedding, and checks for a non-empty chat response. RBAC propagation retries are bounded. Model tokens are billed even during this small test. 
 If that stage fails, no AKS or database provisioning has begun. Fix model access, regional deployment support or quota first. The tool does not silently substitute a different model or change vector dimensions. 
 Stage 02: foundation, then independent long operations 
   infra/foundation.bicep   creates a virtual network with separate AKS, Functions and PostgreSQL subnets; a NAT gateway with a static egress IP; private PostgreSQL DNS; ACR; a storage account and private containers; request/reply queues; Key Vault; App Configuration; five managed identities; and Function telemetry. It explicitly provides outbound connectivity instead of relying on implicit default outbound access. 
 After the foundation is ready, the script creates random PostgreSQL and browser passwords directly in Key Vault. Values are not printed. The PostgreSQL secure ARM parameter is written to a permission-restricted temporary file only while submitting that deployment, then deleted. Never enable shell tracing with  set -x  around these scripts. 
   infra/database.bicep   creates PostgreSQL 17 Flexible Server on the delegated private subnet, a database called  products , and the  VECTOR  extension allowlist setting.   infra/compute.bicep   independently starts one-node AKS with workload identity, OIDC and the KEDA add-on, and a Python 3.12 Flex Consumption Function app integrated into its delegated subnet. 
 Know where traffic can go 
    Connection  Core choice  Why it works      AKS / Function → PostgreSQL  Private VNet address and private DNS  All three dedicated subnets share the VNet. No public database firewall opening is needed.    Workloads → Storage, queues, models, settings, vault  Public HTTPS/TLS service endpoints + Entra identity  NAT provides explicit egress. “Public endpoint” does not mean anonymous access.    Event Grid → Blob extension webhook  Function's public HTTPS endpoint + Blob-extension system key  Registered after code publication; only the manuals container's BlobCreated events match.    Browser → Products  Public load balancer restricted to your IPv4 /32; self-signed TLS + sign-in  Certificate setup happens after the load balancer has an IP. Blob contents remain private.    
 Use the provisioning time 
 The command returns after ARM accepts the two long deployments; it does not claim they are ready. Now continue directly to the Docker chapter. Do not run later dependent stages until  03-ready.sh  confirms both operations. Resume state and non-secret outputs live under  workshop/.state/ . A different terminal still uses the same subscription and group through  common.sh . 
  Verification:  expect the final line to say that AKS/Functions and PostgreSQL are provisioning. This is example/expected behavior. Stage 03 will poll actual deployment states, report failed ARM operations and enforce a 40-minute deadline for each operation. 
 Common failures    A name is already soft-deleted:  inspect the matching Key Vault/App Configuration name. Recover your own workshop resource deliberately, or use a new prefix in a new state folder. Do not purge or adopt someone else's resource.   Resource policy or region denies an SKU:  read the failed ARM operation. Choose a compatible region/SKU in the bootstrap configuration before a new deployment, or have the owner adjust policy. A successful model probe does not grant compute quota.   A rerun finds an existing resource group:  the script verifies its  workshop-id  tag. It refuses to modify a group with a different tag; never work around that by changing another group's tags.   Interrupted stage:  rerun the same stage. Names, role-assignment IDs and secret reuse are deliberate. Check the deployment state before replacing configuration.  
  Continue now:  read and build Products while provisioning runs. You do not need to wait in this chapter.

title: Read, build and run Products
summary: Understand the supplied Spring Boot application and turn its source into a versioned container image.
text:
You will learn:  image versus container, a Dockerfile's build stages, version tags, and the important Java application boundaries.   Starting requirements:  stage 02 has created ACR and begun the slow deployments. Docker can run Linux containers. You receive complete working source; do not rewrite the applications.   Shell and directory:  Bash, repository root. The script selects each correct Docker build context.  
 Read the supplied application first 
 Open   apps/products/src/main/java/org/tubalabs/products/ProductsController.java  . The upload endpoint validates the name and UTF-8  .txt  file, creates a product with a random product ID and manual ID, then uploads to  manuals/products/<productId>/<manualId>.txt . It includes both IDs and a checksum in blob metadata. The IDs are stable for that upload; a different product receives new ones. 
 Open   apps/products/src/main/java/org/tubalabs/products/Store.java  . Notice the explicit SQL,  JdbcClient , and the small transaction that writes a question and its outbox message together. The scheduled   apps/products/src/main/java/org/tubalabs/products/MessagePump.java   sends committed outbox entries and consumes replies. These are separate operations because PostgreSQL and Service Bus do not share one atomic transaction. 
 Thymeleaf templates live under  src/main/resources/templates . They render the upload and chat forms on the server. The browser's   apps/products/src/main/resources/static/app.js   sends requests, polls persistent states and renders text safely using  textContent . It does not call Azure models or hold Azure credentials. 
 Understand the two-stage Dockerfile 
   apps/products/Dockerfile  Copy    FROM maven:3.9.11-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B dependency:go-offline
COPY src src
RUN mvn -B package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21.0.9_10-jre-jammy
RUN groupadd --gid 10001 app && useradd --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /src/target/products.jar app.jar
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080 8443
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=65", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
    Source:   apps/products/Dockerfile   
 The first  FROM  supplies Maven and Java 21.  WORKDIR  selects the container's build directory. Copying  pom.xml  before the source lets Docker cache dependency downloads. Maven creates  target/products.jar . The second stage copies only the JAR into a JRE image and runs as an unprivileged user. 
 An  image  is the packaged, versioned filesystem and startup configuration. A  container  is a running instance of an image.  EXPOSE  documents ports; it does not publish them.  -p  on  docker run  publishes a port. AKS later runs the same image as a container inside a Pod. 
 Build, tag and push both images 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/05-images.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The stage performs  docker build  for Products and ProductsChat, authenticates Docker to ACR with your Azure sign-in, then performs  docker push . The tag looks like  w1-…  and is derived from the build inputs, not  latest . The registry name comes from the shared configuration. You do not replace hostnames throughout the tutorial. 
 Read   scripts/05-images.sh  :  -t registry/name:tag  assigns the full image reference during the build. Giving an existing image another name uses  docker tag ; it does not rebuild or copy its layers. A tag can move; a digest identifies content. Do not overwrite workshop tags after publishing them. 
 Products' context is its own directory. The worker context is the repository root so it can include the small shared Python package; the root  .dockerignore  excludes everything except its required inputs. No  .state , secret files, local virtual environments or build credentials enter either image. 
 Run a container without Azure connections 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    tag=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("workshop/.state/images.json"))["tag"])')
registry=$(python3 -c 'import json; print(json.load(open("workshop/.state/config.json"))["stem"]+"acr.azurecr.io")')
docker run --rm --name products-inspect -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  "$registry/products:$tag" --spring.profiles.active=inspect
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 In another Bash terminal, run  curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8080/  and  curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8080/actuator/health/liveness . The first response explicitly says  Inspect profile . This profile exposes startup information and health only; upload/chat and Azure connections are disabled. It is a Docker exercise, not a simulated Azure deployment. 
 Use  docker ps  to see the running container and  docker logs products-inspect  to inspect Java startup. Stop it with  Ctrl+C ;  --rm  removes this disposable container. The cloud deployment uses the  azure  profile and requires real dependencies. 
  Optional: practice a separate docker tag command or compile with Wrapper  Use the same  tag  and  registry  variables from the run block, then run  docker tag "$registry/products:$tag" products-local:$tag . Inspect it with  docker image inspect "products-local:$tag" . The image ID matches. For a local Java build, change to  workshop/apps/products  and run  bash mvnw test  with Java 21. Database integration tests require the disposable PostgreSQL fixture described on the maintainer page.  
 Expected behavior and common fixes 
  Verification:  both pushes finish with a registry digest, the inspect container responds on localhost, and its health response is  {"status":"UP"} . These are expected outputs; see the validation report for checks actually run by the maintainer. 
   ACR push returns denied:  rerun  az acr login  through the stage and confirm your subscription has registry push rights. Registry administrator credentials are intentionally disabled.   Port 8080 is occupied:  use  127.0.0.1:8081:8080  for this local run and curl port 8081. The AKS manifest still uses its own port 8443.   Build download fails:  check Docker's internet/proxy access and rerun. Layers cache completed work; do not change library versions just to mask a transient repository failure.   Exec format error:  rebuild with the supplied  --platform linux/amd64  flag and confirm Docker supports that platform.  
  Continue when:  the images are in ACR and the local inspect run works. Now wait for Azure readiness and connect the real services.

title: Connect data, settings and identity
summary: Configure private PostgreSQL, Flyway, private blobs, Key Vault secrets and App Configuration settings.
text:
You will learn:  schema migration versus data, vector shape, private networking, and the distinction between settings, secrets and identity.   Starting requirements:  stages 01–02 were submitted successfully; images have been built. Slow provisioning may still be running.   Shell and directory:  Bash, repository root. The scripts isolate kubectl in  workshop/.state/kubeconfig ; set that path explicitly for manual kubectl commands.  
 Wait, then configure access 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/03-ready.sh
bash workshop/scripts/04-configure.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
  03-ready.sh  waits for actual ARM completion, reports failed operations, gets this cluster's credentials into its own kubeconfig, waits for a Ready node and checks the PostgreSQL extension allowlist. It does not open a public PostgreSQL firewall rule. Your laptop normally cannot connect directly to the private database. 
  04-configure.sh  assigns data-plane roles, creates federated credentials, grants the kubelet identity  AcrPull , configures KEDA's own identity, and writes ordinary settings. It retries boundedly for directory/RBAC propagation. Resource creation permissions do not automatically grant a workload permission to read a blob, secret, setting or queue. 
 Follow identity to settings and secrets 
   AKS service account Annotated client ID + labeled Pod  →   Federated identity AKS OIDC token exchanged for Entra token  →   App Configuration Endpoints, deployments, counts  →   Key Vault Retrieve actual database/browser passwords  Functions uses its assigned managed identity directly. Every application's ordinary settings and secrets are read once at startup.  
 AKS workload identity requires all three: the service account's  azure.workload.identity/client-id  annotation, the Pod's  azure.workload.identity/use: "true"  label, and an Azure federated credential with the exact issuer, subject and audience. The webhook injects token-file/environment bootstrap. See   k8s/products.yaml   and   scripts/04-configure.sh  . 
 The only application-specific bootstrap environment settings are  APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT  and its  workshop  label. The SDK credential uses the workload/managed identity. App Configuration supplies the Key Vault URI and ordinary service settings. Then the application reads the PostgreSQL password from Key Vault. The Java application also reads its browser sign-in password there. These values are not Kubernetes environment variables or image layers. 
    Mechanism  What this workshop puts there  What it does not do      Key Vault  Actual PostgreSQL and Products sign-in passwords  Does not replace the application's database connection or encrypt its SQL automatically    App Configuration  Endpoints, model deployment names, retrieval count, chunk size  Is not used as a password store    Kubernetes ConfigMap  The non-secret App Configuration endpoint and label  Is not a secret manager    Kubernetes Secret  The demo endpoint's TLS certificate/private key  Is not Key Vault; access still depends on Kubernetes RBAC    Environment variables  Bootstrap selectors and SDK-injected identity metadata  Are a process input mechanism, not a secure secret service    Managed/workload identity  Short-lived tokens tied to the Function or service account  Does not grant permissions until Azure roles are assigned    
 Read the Flyway migration 
 Products runs the supplied Flyway migration during startup, before serving application requests. Flyway records its version/checksum in  flyway_schema_history . A second startup validates/reuses the existing migration; do not edit an applied migration to change a live schema. 
   apps/products/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__products_and_messages.sql   creates  vector  and the product, chunk, chat, outbox and result-cache tables. PostgreSQL must first allowlist  VECTOR ; Bicep does that at server level. Flyway then runs as  workshopadmin , the database owner created by this workshop. That account can create the allowlisted extension and all tables. 
 The core deliberately uses the same database owner's credentials in all three applications to keep the first deployment small. They are stored only in Key Vault and retrieved at startup. This grants broader database access than a production application should have. Independent migration/runtime SQL roles or Entra PostgreSQL authentication are optional extensions, not secretly assumed setup. 
    Invariant  Implementation      Document/question vector agreement  Both call the  embedding  deployment and request 1536 dimensions; the table is  vector(1536) . Code rejects non-finite or incorrectly sized vectors.    Retry-safe chunks  Primary key  (manual_id, chunk_index) ; all chunk writes and the ready state commit atomically.    Simple retrieval  Exact cosine scan using  <=> , optional product ID filter, configurable count and minimum similarity.    Persistent asynchronous chat  Questions + outbox commit together; worker results are cached by request ID; terminal replies cannot overwrite a displayed answer.    
 Notice upload ordering 
 The product row commits  before  Blob upload starts. If upload fails, Products marks the record failed. If a process dies between those operations, the record may remain waiting; the timeout sweep marks old work failed. A participant retries by creating a new product/manual, not by mutating the old blob. The embedder checks the stored checksum and IDs before indexing. 
  Optional: inspect the full SQL or think about production changes    apps/products/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__products_and_messages.sql  Copy    -- Azure must allowlist VECTOR before Flyway runs. Run as the database owner.
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE products (
    id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    name varchar(120) NOT NULL,
    manual_id uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    blob_name text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    manual_sha256 char(64) NOT NULL,
    status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'waiting'
        CHECK (status IN ('waiting', 'processing', 'ready', 'failed')),
    error text,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- No ANN index: an exact cosine scan is easier to inspect for three manuals.
CREATE TABLE manual_chunks (
    manual_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES products(manual_id),
    product_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
    chunk_index integer NOT NULL CHECK (chunk_index >= 0),
    content text NOT NULL,
    embedding vector(1536) NOT NULL,
    embedding_deployment text NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (manual_id, chunk_index)
);
CREATE INDEX manual_chunks_product ON manual_chunks(product_id);

CREATE TABLE chat_requests (
    id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
    correlation_id uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    product_id uuid REFERENCES products(id),
    question varchar(1000) NOT NULL,
    status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued'
        CHECK (status IN ('queued', 'processing', 'completed', 'failed')),
    answer text,
    sources jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',
    error text,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    deadline timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now() + interval '8 minutes',
    updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Commit the request and its outgoing message together. A crash after sending
-- may resend it; the worker's persistent result cache handles that duplicate.
CREATE TABLE chat_outbox (
    request_id uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES chat_requests(id),
    payload jsonb NOT NULL,
    sent_at timestamptz,
    attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE TABLE chat_results (
    request_id uuid PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES chat_requests(id),
    correlation_id uuid NOT NULL,
    payload jsonb NOT NULL,
    created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
    Source:   apps/products/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__products_and_messages.sql    The small dataset does not justify an approximate-nearest-neighbor index. For a large corpus, compare an exact scan with HNSW/IVFFlat, recall, memory and query plans. An index is a measured optimization, not a required RAG decoration.  
 Verification and common failures 
  Verification:  stage 03 should report a Ready node and  VECTOR ; stage 04 should finish configuration without printing secret values. Flyway runs in the next chapter when Products starts. No fabricated SQL output is presented here. 
   PostgreSQL hostname resolves publicly or not at all inside a Pod:  inspect the private DNS zone's VNet link and the database's delegated subnet. Do not solve it with a public  0.0.0.0/0  firewall rule.   Key Vault / App Configuration returns 403:  check the workload's principal ID and the exact resource scope; wait for the bounded propagation retries. A CLI login as yourself does not configure the Pod identity.   Flyway cannot create vector:  check  azure.extensions  and confirm you are using the configured database owner. Do not use  pgvector  as the SQL extension name; the extension is  vector .   KEDA later shows authentication errors:  the scaler has a separate identity/federated credential, not the worker's service account. Its configuration is completed here for the later exercise.  
  Continue when:  the cluster, database, identities and ordinary settings are ready. Next, deploy Products and observe Flyway startup.

title: Deploy Products to AKS
summary: Read a Deployment, Pod and Service; then open a restricted HTTPS endpoint and inspect its rollout.
text:
You will learn:  the relationship between a Deployment, Pod, Service, probes and a rollout.   Starting requirements:  stages 03–05 pass; images exist in ACR and the kubelet can pull them.   Shell and directory:  Bash, repository root. For manual commands use  export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/workshop/.state/kubeconfig"  in each new terminal.  
 Read the Kubernetes resources 
   k8s/products.yaml   declares a namespace, an annotated service account, a bootstrap ConfigMap and a Deployment with  one replica . The Deployment controller keeps the desired Pod running. A Pod is the smallest Kubernetes scheduling unit; here it contains one Java container. Its labels connect the Deployment selector, the Service and the identity webhook. 
 The Pod requests 500 millicores and 768 MiB so the scheduler can reserve capacity; its larger limits bound usage. Startup allows time for configuration, PostgreSQL connection and Flyway migration. Readiness includes database health; liveness checks whether the process is alive. A temporary database outage should remove the Pod from ready traffic rather than cause a liveness restart loop. 
   k8s/service.yaml   is a  LoadBalancer  Service: a stable entry point whose selector finds Products Pods. Port 443 forwards to the container's HTTPS port 8443. It restricts callers to the configured public IPv4  /32 . A Service forwards traffic; it does not run application code. 
 Create the endpoint and deploy 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/06-products.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The script applies the namespace and Service first, waits boundedly for the public IP, and generates a short-lived self-signed certificate for that IP. It installs the certificate/private key as a Kubernetes TLS Secret, renders only known non-secret manifest values, applies the Deployment, waits for rollout and checks HTTPS readiness using the saved certificate. 
   Endpoint assumptions:  this is a real public HTTPS endpoint, restricted by source IP and requiring sign-in. Its certificate is self-signed and valid for two days. Compare the script's SHA-256 fingerprint with the browser's certificate before accepting the warning. Do not disable TLS verification globally. The supplied tools trust only  workshop/.state/tls.crt . Production needs a trusted certificate, DNS, SSO and an access design.  
 The script prints the actual URL and saves it in  .state/endpoint.txt . Open it in your browser. Use username  participant . Deliberately retrieve the random password with  bash workshop/scripts/credentials.sh  in your own interactive terminal; the helper refuses redirected output. Do not paste the password into this documentation site's search, progress storage or a URL. 
 Inspect a working rollout 
 After setting this terminal's kubeconfig as above, run  kubectl get deployment,pods,service -n products . Expect one ready Products replica, a Pod whose name was generated by the Deployment, and a load balancer IP. Run  kubectl logs deployment/products -n products --tail=50  and find the Flyway schema creation/validation and Java startup lines. The exact Pod name and output will differ. 
 Use  kubectl describe pod -n products -l app=products  to inspect events, identity-injected variables, mounted volumes and probe configuration. Pod events explain image-pull, scheduling and readiness failures more directly than repeatedly refreshing the browser. 
 Try  kubectl rollout restart deployment/products -n products  followed by  kubectl rollout status deployment/products -n products --timeout=300s . It starts a new Pod from the same image and persisted database; Flyway should not create the schema again. The core has one node, so a rolling update depends on the spare capacity left by the small resource requests. 
 Open Upload product, but do not index yet 
 The empty product list and upload form should render. It is possible to upload now, but Event Grid is not subscribed until the next chapter. To avoid a stranded demonstration upload, wait until the Function and subscription are ready before creating your first product. Event Grid does not automatically replay a BlobCreated event that happened before the subscription existed. 
  Verification:  open the real URL, sign in, and see both “Upload product” and “Chat about products”. The readiness request must report  UP . Restart Products once and confirm it returns ready with its existing schema. 
 Common failures and exact next checks    ImagePullBackOff:  use  kubectl describe pod ; compare the rendered ACR image/tag with the push and verify the kubelet principal's AcrPull assignment. The workload's blob identity does not pull the image.   CrashLoopBackOff:  run  kubectl logs -n products deployment/products --previous  if a container restarted. Check App Configuration, Key Vault and private PostgreSQL reachability in that order.   Browser cannot reach the IP:  confirm the current network still has the configured public IPv4. A changed VPN/egress IP will be blocked. Update  allowedCidr  to the new exact /32 and rerun the stage; never replace it with the entire internet.   Certificate expires:  rerun stage 06; it regenerates a near-expiry certificate. Restart Products to load a changed mounted certificate, then compare its new fingerprint.   403 on a write API:  CSRF protection remains enabled. The UI uses it automatically; smoke/load clients first request a session token from  /api/csrf .  
  Continue when:  Products is ready and accessible. Next, connect the upload event to actual embedding work.

title: Turn a manual into vectors
summary: Deploy a Python Function whose Event Grid-backed Blob trigger chunks and indexes an immutable manual safely.
text:
You will learn:  Python's small functions, the difference between an event and file contents, chunking, embeddings and retry-safe persistence.   Starting requirements:  Products is deployed, Flyway ran, and the Azure model probe passed. Do not upload the first manual until this chapter's subscription is ready.   Shell and directory:  Bash, repository root. Activate  workshop/.tools/venv  for the optional sample/replay tools.  
 Understand the trigger before publishing 
 Read   apps/products-embedder/function_app.py  . The decorator declares a  blobTrigger , connection prefix  ManualStorage , path matching  manuals/products/{productId}/{manualId}.txt , and  source='EventGrid' . Azure Functions' Blob extension handles the notification and reads the file; the Python function receives an  InputStream . It extracts stable IDs from the path and passes bytes to the small indexing helper. 
 Our explicit Event Grid subscription filters BlobCreated notifications to this container/path and  .txt  suffix. Its destination is the Function's  Blob-extension webhook , not an ordinary HTTP trigger or a Service Bus queue. The Blob-extension system key protects that webhook; the script handles it without printing it or saving it in the website. 
 Flex Consumption supports Python 3.12, VNet integration and the Event Grid source for Blob triggers. It uses a blob deployment container rather than Azure Files. The template supplies the deployment identity, identity-based  AzureWebJobsStorage , Blob/Queue connection endpoints, the delegated subnet and telemetry settings. Host storage is infrastructure for the Functions runtime, distinct from the manual that your code indexes. 
 Publish code and connect notifications 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/07-embedder.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The packaging helper gathers the real Python sources and canonical requirements into a ZIP. Azure CLI requests a remote Linux build and package deployment; Windows-built native packages are not uploaded. The stage then creates a Storage system topic, grants its dead-letter identity access to the private dead-letter container, waits for the  blobs_extension  host key, and registers the filtered webhook. 
 “Serverless” still means code runs on servers. The platform manages those servers and invocation scaling. It does not remove the need for host storage, a deployment package, identity roles, networking or timeout handling. 
 Upload a supplied manual 
 Return to Products →  Upload product . Use product name  Aurora Trail Lamp  and download/select  aurora-trail-lamp.txt . Upload it once. The row should move through  waiting ,  processing  and  ready ; a quick run may make an intermediate state too brief to notice. Upload completion and embedding completion are separate events. 
 Then upload  Cedar Desk Fan  using  its manual , and  Harbor Travel Kettle  using  its manual . Distinctive specifications make later retrieval objectively inspectable. The manuals are short fictional data, not manufacturer safety guidance. 
 Read the chunking and indexing code 
   apps/shared/rag_core/chunks.py   uses readable loops, string slices and paragraph/sentence/whitespace boundaries. It caps chunks at the configured character count and includes a little overlap so a boundary is less likely to separate a specification from its product name. Characters are a simple workshop approximation, not the model's tokenizer. 
   apps/shared/rag_core/models.py   calls the Azure-hosted embedding deployment with the identity token and explicitly requests  1536 dimensions . Both this Function and the chat worker use that same deployment and dimension. The embedding response is a list of numbers, not a text answer. 
   apps/shared/rag_core/embedding.py   takes a per-manual PostgreSQL advisory lock. It verifies the record and checksum, commits the visible processing state, obtains embeddings, and writes all chunks and the ready state in one transaction. The uniqueness rule is  (manual_id, chunk_index) . A ready manual returns without calling the model again. Failed attempts persist a safe error and raise so the Functions extension can retry; repeated failures eventually reach its poison queue. 
 This protects against repeated notifications and crashes around persistence. It is not a claim of exactly-once event delivery. Immutable blob paths keep event versioning understandable; replacing a blob under the same path violates the core path's checksum rule. 
 Inspect counts and dimensions, not huge vectors 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/inspect-data.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The script runs a bounded Job inside the VNet, using the worker's identity and configuration. It prints each product/manual ID, status, number of chunks, and minimum/maximum vector dimensions. Expect nonzero chunks and dimensions  1536  for every ready manual. The actual chunk count depends on text and the configured size. No 1536-number arrays or passwords are dumped. 
  Verification:  all three manuals are ready; their chunk counts are positive; minimum and maximum vector dimensions are both 1536. Use these actual observations before continuing to chat. 
 Two small, observable exercises 
   Change a manual:  save a copy of Aurora's file, change  420 lumens  to  510 lumens , and call it revision B in its text. Upload it as a  new  product named “Aurora Trail Lamp Rev B”. Keep both products. In the next chapter, selecting each product should retrieve its own specification.   Observe duplicate handling:  while the verification virtual environment is active, run  python workshop/tools/replay_event.py  to replay a ready manual's BlobCreated event twice. Then rerun the data inspection. Counts should be unchanged. The Blob extension can suppress a duplicate through its receipt; if application code runs, its ready/checksum guard independently prevents extra rows. Local integration tests exercise that code path directly.  
 Common failures and fixes    Manual stays waiting:  confirm the event subscription exists and is Succeeded, the source container/path matches, and IndexManual appears in the Function list. Upload a  new  product if the original upload preceded subscription creation.   No host key or Function discovery:  inspect remote build logs, the 4.x extension bundle and the managed identity's Storage Blob Data Owner, Queue Data Contributor and Account Contributor roles. Those host permissions are broader than merely reading a manual.   Manual fails during indexing:  inspect Function traces by manual ID in Application Insights. Check database DNS/connectivity, model RBAC/quota and vector dimensions. Inspect  webjobs-blobtrigger-poison  in the host storage queues after repeated failures.   Event delivery fails permanently:  inspect the private  event-deadletters  blob container and the system topic identity's role. Event Grid dead letters and the Function Blob-trigger poison queue are different failure locations.  
  Continue when:  at least the original three supplied manuals are ready and have 1536-dimensional chunks. Now the worker can retrieve real evidence.

title: Ask a grounded question
summary: Follow a persistent question through Service Bus, vector retrieval, the model and a correlated reply.
text:
You will learn:  persistent asynchronous request/reply, correlation, vector retrieval, grounding and safe retries.   Starting requirements:  Products works; the supplied manuals are ready; request/reply queues and all identity assignments exist.   Shell and directory:  Bash, repository root. Use  workshop/.state/kubeconfig  for manual Kubernetes commands.  
 Start one worker first 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/08-chat.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The stage applies   k8s/chat.yaml  , temporarily starts one worker and waits for readiness. It verifies App Configuration, Key Vault and database startup before KEDA takes over in the next chapter. Products still runs separately with one replica. 
 Read   apps/products-chat/worker.py  . A context manager opens a Service Bus receiver and sender. Each pod handles one request at a time with  prefetch zero . It validates the JSON body against its expected fields and checks message ID/correlation headers against the persistent identifiers. No model key is present; model and Azure service calls use identity tokens. 
 Follow the persistent protocol 
    Step  Persisted behavior      Submit  Products stores question, optional product, request ID, correlation ID, an eight-minute deadline and an outbox entry in one PostgreSQL transaction. The browser receives HTTP 202.    Dispatch  The sender publishes the outbox body to  chat-requests , with message ID=request ID and matching correlation ID. It marks the outbox sent only after sending.    Process  The worker changes queued → processing, embeds the question, retrieves evidence and generates an answer. It caches the reply in PostgreSQL before publishing.    Reply  The worker sends to  chat-replies . Products checks the correlation and commits the terminal answer/sources before acknowledging the reply.    Poll  The browser polls Products by request ID. Refreshing the chat URL resumes polling that database record; no open HTTP request has to survive.    
 The exact message contracts are   contracts/chat-request.schema.json   and   contracts/chat-reply.schema.json  . Request and correlation IDs are both persisted UUIDs. The worker compares the message with the stored question/product so a body/header mismatch is rejected, not silently associated with another request. 
 Read the small RAG implementation 
   apps/shared/rag_core/chat.py   contains the direct SQL query: join ready products to chunks, optionally filter the product ID, compute cosine similarity using  1 - (embedding <=> question_vector) , filter by minimum similarity, order by distance and take the configured count. There is no orchestration framework and no approximate vector index. 
 The model helper sends a short application instruction and inspectable JSON containing the question and retrieved reference data. It asks for numbered citations and an explicit insufficient-information response when the sources cannot support an answer. The application exposes the actual retrieved passages. If retrieval has no useful evidence, it returns the insufficient-information answer without a chat call. If the generated answer has no valid cited reference, the application also falls back to that answer. 
   Untrusted manuals:  text in a manual or question is not allowed to override application instructions, reveal secrets or call tools. The worker does not offer tools or access to additional documents to the model. Prompt separation and evidence checks reduce risks; they are not a guarantee that a model can never make an incorrect claim.  
 Ask questions you can check 
  In Products → Chat, select  Aurora Trail Lamp  and ask: “What is the operating temperature of the Aurora Trail Lamp?” The supporting passage should include “−10 to 40 degrees Celsius” (the supplied plain text uses  -10 ).  Select  Cedar Desk Fan  and ask how to enable its timer. Check for the two-second hold and 45-minute duration in the returned source, not just in the generated sentence.  Select  Harbor Travel Kettle  and ask whether it works on a 110 V supply. The manual explicitly says 220–240 V only and not dual voltage.  Ask: “What is the CEO's private telephone number?” The manuals provide no evidence. Expect an explicit insufficient-information answer, not an invented number.  
   samples/questions.json   records the questions and expected supporting passages. LLM wording is nondeterministic; verification checks evidence and source IDs rather than a fixed answer string. If you uploaded Aurora revision B, select each revision separately and ask about lumens: the product filter should prevent cross-product mixing. 
 Change an ordinary setting 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/change-retrieval.sh 1
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 This changes  rag:retrieval-count  from 3 to 1 in App Configuration and restarts the worker deployment.  Refresh is not implemented.  Settings and secrets are read once at process startup in both Python applications and Products. For the Function, a changed chunk setting requires a Function app restart; for Products, a changed bootstrap/secret requires its rollout restart. A stored result remains cached and is not regenerated. 
 Ask a  new  question after restart and verify that the worker startup log says  retrieval_count=1  and at most one cited passage appears. Restore 3 by running  bash workshop/scripts/change-retrieval.sh 3 . At zero replicas later, the changed pod template takes effect when KEDA starts a new worker. 
 Know what acknowledgement means 
 A receive operation locks a Service Bus message temporarily; it does not remove it.  Complete  acknowledges successful processing.  Abandon  makes it available for retry. A lost lock or expired receiver can also cause redelivery. The queue starts with a one-minute lock, while automatic lock renewal in the worker allows up to ten minutes for slow model calls. Requests still have their own eight-minute application deadline. 
 Repeated processing failures produce a safe failed reply and a dead-lettered request. The broker also dead-letters messages after its configured maximum deliveries or TTL. Products persists timeouts independently, so a lost reply does not leave an endless spinner. Inspect the request ID in logs and the dead-letter subqueue; increasing delivery count alone does not fix bad credentials or model quota. 
 There is an intentional at-least-once window between sending and marking an outbox entry, and between replying and acknowledging a request. A per-request advisory lock and persistent result cache avoid repeated displayed answers and normally avoid repeat LLM calls after a cached result. A crash before caching can repeat a model call. Terminal reply updates are guarded by request/correlation/deadline. This is  not exactly-once delivery . 
  Verification:  see queued/processing/completed states, a non-empty answer and relevant passages. Refresh the request URL: it should show the same persisted answer. Confirm the unsupported question is refused. 
 Common failures    Queued forever:  inspect Products' outbox warnings, request queue counts and worker readiness. Check queue-scoped Sender/Receiver roles and the correct namespace.   Processing then failed:  inspect worker logs by request ID; check model 429 throttling, model deployment names, database access and lock renewal. The browser shows a persisted error or timeout.   Wrong product's passage:  check the selected product ID and source IDs. An unfiltered question can legitimately retrieve multiple manuals; a filtered one must not.   Manual instructions appear to influence behavior:  inspect the prompt and references. Do not add unsafe content or broaden tool access to make an unsupported answer work.  
  Continue when:  grounded questions, unsupported questions and the retrieval-count change are observable. Next, let queue metrics control worker replicas.

title: Make the queue drive scaling
summary: Observe zero workers, a bounded backlog, multiple workers, completed answers and a return to zero.
text:
You will learn:  KEDA's scaler identity, queue metrics, activation, HPA scaling and scale-to-zero.   Starting requirements:  at least one manual is ready and a single chat worker successfully answered a question. There should be no unrelated requests waiting.   Shell and directory:  two Bash terminals, both at the repository root. The producer terminal has  workshop/.tools/venv  activated; the observer uses the supplied script's isolated kubeconfig.  
 Give scaling to KEDA 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/09-keda.sh
bash workshop/scripts/demo-scaling.sh start
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
   k8s/keda.yaml   defines a  TriggerAuthentication  with the  KEDA identity's client ID  and a  ScaledObject  targeting only  products-chat . The scaler polls every 10 seconds, activates on any active request, targets two active messages per worker, allows zero to three replicas, and uses a 60-second cooldown. HPA scale-down stabilization can add another observation delay. 
 KEDA reads event-source metrics and changes desired replica counts. It does not receive questions or run RAG processing. The worker still consumes and acknowledges messages. The KEDA operator needs its own federated credential, service-account annotation, Pod label and Service Bus Data Receiver role; the worker identity does not automatically supply these. 
 The demo switch enables an explicit  20-second per-request delay  so the small, bounded backlog remains visible long enough for scaling. It is off in the normal worker manifest. No extra artificial LLM requests are hidden in the delay. Turn it off after the exercise. 
 Terminal A: watch a complete cycle 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/watch-scaling.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 First wait until the chat deployment reaches  zero . Products should stay at one. The observer runs for at most eight minutes; Ctrl+C stops only the observer. It shows deployment replica counts and the request queue's active/dead-letter counts. Azure management counts are sampled and may lag; compare several observations. 
 Terminal B: submit bounded work 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
source workshop/.tools/venv/bin/activate
python workshop/tools/load.py --count 8
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The tool submits  eight  persisted questions through Products, using a ready manual, then waits boundedly for all replies. It refuses more than twelve. Each uncached request normally makes one question embedding call and one chat call, so tokens are billed. This is a scaling exercise, not a throughput benchmark. 
   Idle:  chat replicas are 0, request backlog is 0, Products remains 1.   Arrival:  active messages appear after Products dispatches the committed outbox.   Activation:  KEDA starts a worker after its next successful poll.   Scale-out:  enough backlog remains for HPA to request more than one worker, capped at 3.   Completion:  the producer prints completed request IDs; active backlog drains.   Cooldown:  after idle metrics, cooldown and stabilization, workers return to 0.  
 These are the required  observations to make on your deployment , not fabricated captured output. Note the actual maximum replica count and the rough time back to zero in your walkthrough notes. Use the  maintainer checklist  if a phase is not visible. 
 Change the threshold and compare 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/demo-scaling.sh threshold 4
python workshop/tools/load.py --count 8
bash workshop/scripts/demo-scaling.sh stop
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 After the first cycle is idle, target four messages per worker rather than two and send the same bounded load. Expect less aggressive scale-out under comparable backlog; exact timing depends on model latency and metric polling. The last command disables the delay and reapplies the normal scaler settings. Do not leave the demonstration delay enabled for ordinary use. 
 Why this fits one node 
 One D4ds_v5 node has four vCPUs and 16 GiB before system reservations. Products requests 500m CPU / 768 MiB, each worker 250m / 384 MiB; three workers plus Products leave room for system components and a rollout. Node autoscaling is disabled. A pending Pod means inspect allocatable capacity and existing workloads rather than assuming KEDA must also create nodes. 
  Queue depth  determines the desired scale.  Concurrency  is one request per worker here.  Prefetch  is zero so a worker does not lock a large invisible backlog in its local buffer.  Model quota  can throttle additional workers: scaling above quota may increase retries, not throughput.  Cooldown  is intentionally short for this exercise; cold starts still take time. 
  Verification:  observe all six phases, all eight completed answers, no new dead letters, and Products still serving at one replica. Disable the delay. If you only observed one worker, investigate and repeat the bounded exercise before marking this chapter complete. 
 Common failures    ScaledObject Ready=False or 401/403:  describe it and inspect  kube-system/keda-operator  logs. Check the operator's identity/federated subject, not just the chat service account. Rerun stage 04 after correcting assignments.   Workers never reach zero:  check queue backlog, active requests, cooldown/stabilization and whether another manual scaling command or controller is competing. Do not manually keep replicas at one after handing control to KEDA.   Only one worker appears:  verify the 20-second delay applied to new pods, threshold=2 and prefetch=0. Check HPA metrics and watch long enough. Do not turn the load generator into an infinite loop.   Pods Pending:  describe the Pod and inspect node allocatable resources. Keep the supplied resource requests and maximum three workers; quota expansion is not needed for this bounded example.   Model 429:  lower the scaler maximum/producer count or obtain model quota. More replicas cannot overcome a service token limit.  
  Continue when:  you have seen a full scaling cycle and restored normal settings. Next run the final smoke test and clean up.

title: Verify, diagnose and clean up
summary: Run the real-deployment smoke test, diagnose failures and deliberately remove only workshop resources.
text:
You will learn:  how to verify an asynchronous system without guessing model wording, locate its separate failure queues and remove resources deliberately.   Starting requirements:  all core components are deployed, KEDA is Ready, the demo delay is disabled and the sample manuals are indexed.   Shell and directory:  Bash, repository root; activate the verification virtual environment in this terminal.  
 Run the real-deployment acceptance check 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    # shellcheck source=/dev/null
source workshop/.tools/venv/bin/activate
python workshop/tools/smoke.py
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
   tools/smoke.py   first checks ARM deployment states, the Ready Products rollout, Function discovery, event subscription and queue configuration. It verifies database readiness through Products, uploads a new Aurora manual, waits up to seven minutes for indexing, submits a temperature question with a product filter, and waits up to eight minutes for its persisted reply. 
 It checks the request/correlation IDs, a non-empty answer and a returned passage containing the known temperature specification with the correct product/manual IDs. It does  not  assert exact LLM wording. Its non-secret result report is saved under  .state/smoke-result.json . Passwords stay in process memory, TLS verification uses the exact local certificate, and no credential is placed in a URL. 
  Verification:  expect the tool to report a real upload → Function indexing → queue/worker → correlated answer with relevant references. That line counts as a successful deployment check only if the tool actually ran successfully in your subscription. Consult the  validation report  for the maintainer's observed results. 
 Diagnose the failing boundary 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/diagnostics.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
    Symptom  Inspect  Concrete action      Upload failed  Products logs and its waiting/failed row  Check its Blob Data Contributor role and storage endpoint. Retry as a new product after the cause is fixed.    Waiting manual  Event subscription filter/delivery and Function discovery  Verify the private manuals container/path, Blob-extension webhook key and code publication. A pre-subscription upload needs a new product or a deliberate replay.    Failed indexing  Function telemetry, host poison queue, PostgreSQL connectivity  Use the manual ID in logs; fix model quota/identity/dimensions, then replay the immutable blob. Never change a ready manual in place.    Queued question  Outbox warnings, request queue, ScaledObject conditions  Check sender/scaler/receiver roles separately. Inspect workload federation and queue namespace.    Processing question  Worker logs, model throttling, message renewal and request deadline  Use the request/correlation IDs. Inspect failed/dead-lettered messages; repair the cause before resubmitting a new question.    Bad answer/source  Selected product, actual chunks and prompt  Read evidence, try a focused product filter and inspect retrieval count. An LLM's plausible sentence is not proof of grounding.    
 Function runtime traces are in the workshop's Application Insights resource. The supplied   infra/function-logs.kql   selects recent manual-ID logs and warnings. It is a small log-inspection example, not a claim that end-to-end OpenTelemetry tracing has been implemented across Java, the Function and the worker. 
 There are three distinct dead-letter/poison locations: Event Grid's private  event-deadletters  blob container, the Blob extension's  webjobs-blobtrigger-poison  host-storage queue, and each Service Bus queue's  $DeadLetterQueue  subqueue. A message arriving in one does not imply that the next component ever ran. Avoid dumping event-subscription destination URLs: the Blob webhook URL contains its system key. 
 Deliberately clean up 
   Bash · repository root  Copy    bash workshop/scripts/cleanup.sh
    Canonical commands:   commands.sh   
 The cleanup tool checks the exact subscription and workshop group tag, lists the resources it will delete, names AKS's managed node resource group, and requires you to type  DELETE  plus the complete group name. It only requests deletion of the tagged workshop group; AKS removes its managed node group as part of its lifecycle. It never deletes arbitrary similarly named groups. 
 Deletion is asynchronous. Run the exact  az group exists  command printed by the tool until it returns  false , and verify the managed node group is gone. Azure locks or policy can prevent cleanup; inspect the failed operation instead of assuming costs have stopped. 
 Key Vault secrets/vault remain soft-deleted for seven days; App Configuration uses a one-day soft-delete period. No automatic purge is performed. Names may not be immediately reusable. This workshop does not create resources in an existing shared group. Resource-provider registration remains at subscription level and is intentionally not unregistered. 
 After Azure confirms deletion, remove the local  workshop/.state  directory if you no longer need its non-secret notes, kubeconfig and short-lived TLS private key. Review the exact directory before any recursive deletion. Keep the repository source and documentation; the website itself can still run with no Azure access. 
 What you have exercised 
  Built, tagged, run and pushed a Java container, then inspected its AKS Deployment, Pod, Service, probes and rollout.  Used Flyway and PostgreSQL/pgvector for products, chunks, persistent work and explicit vector retrieval.  Separated Blob notifications/Event Grid/Functions from queued application communication through Service Bus.  Configured workload/managed identity, real Key Vault secrets and ordinary App Configuration settings with explicit restart behavior.  Observed KEDA scale only the worker from zero and back, with a finite producer and finite token spend.  
  Optional extensions after the first successful walkthrough  Add trusted TLS and Entra sign-in, separate migration/runtime database roles, private endpoints for public Azure services, retries with backoff/jitter and richer operational dashboards, manual-version lifecycle, tested token-aware chunking, or measured ANN indexing. Keep each extension separate from the working core baseline.  
 Before you finish  If smoke failed, retain the printed IDs and use the  first-run checklist  to record the failing boundary. If cleanup is still running or blocked, keep monitoring costs. Marking a documentation chapter complete does not perform cleanup or validate Azure.

title: Versions, decisions and sources
summary: Architecture decisions, selected exam objectives, costs and official documentation.
text:
Implementation decisions 
 The core deliberately favors explicit code: Java 21, supported Spring Boot, Maven Wrapper, JdbcClient/SQL, Thymeleaf and Flyway; Python 3.12, direct Azure SDK clients and small HTTP model calls; PostgreSQL 17 and an exact pgvector cosine scan. Application folders can later become separate repositories. The tiny shared Python package can be published as a versioned internal wheel or copied into each Python repository; the current Function ZIP and worker image include the same canonical package. 
 PostgreSQL is private to the VNet, with a delegated subnet and private DNS. AKS and Functions use explicit NAT egress for public, identity-protected Azure endpoints. Storage containers are private and shared-key access is disabled. This core avoids private endpoints for every service and avoids a multi-day network/security course. 
 One database owner is used by migrations and applications, and TLS  sslmode=require  encrypts PostgreSQL traffic inside the private network. Production should separate runtime/migration roles and use full certificate/hostname verification appropriate to its trust store. The Products endpoint has self-signed HTTPS, a source-IP restriction and a random password. It is not public anonymous HTTP, nor a production SSO implementation. 
 Application settings/secrets are read only on startup. Workers are serial with prefetch zero. Messaging is at-least-once with explicit idempotency. Model calls have finite connect/read timeouts; request deadlines and failure states persist independently of the browser. 
 Version and dependency matrix 
   VERSIONS.md   records the exact direct versions, image tags, API versions and validation-tool versions.   constraints.txt   locks the resolved Python dependency versions; it constrains only packages that each requirements file actually installs. The Maven parent and Azure BOM manage Java dependency versions. 
    Component  Selected baseline      Java / application framework  Java 21; Spring Boot 4.1.2; Maven Wrapper 3.3.4 / Maven 3.9.11    Python  3.12 in the Function and worker; dependencies pinned in canonical requirements + constraints    Data  PostgreSQL 17; SQL extension vector;  vector(1536) ; exact cosine query    Function  Functions v4, Python v2 programming model, 4.x extension bundle, Flex Consumption FC1, managed-identity deployment storage    Models  gpt-5-mini / 2025-08-07 and text-embedding-3-small / 1; Azure OpenAI GA v1 REST endpoints; GlobalStandard SKU    Kubernetes  AKS-supported default version at creation, patch upgrades; bundled KEDA add-on. Check kubectl minor-version skew after deployment.    
 Selected AI-200 objectives 
 Checked against the  official AI-200 study guide  on  11 November 2026 , for the skills dated 7 October 2026. This is a partial exercise mapping, not a coverage guarantee. 
    Exercise  Relevant objective area  Boundary      Build, tag and push  Container images and ACR  Local Docker builds; ACR Tasks is not implemented    Manifests, probes, logs, rollout  AKS deployment and troubleshooting  No Container Apps revisions or App Service deployment    KEDA queue scaling  Event-driven scaling concepts  The guide's KEDA objective names Container Apps; this exercise uses AKS    Flyway, explicit SQL, vectors  PostgreSQL data modeling, queries and RAG with metadata filters  Small exact scans; advanced index tuning is optional    Request/reply and failures  Service Bus processing and dead letters  Queues, not a full topics/subscriptions lab    Blob notification and Function  Event Grid workflows and Function configuration/deployment  Blob triggers, not a general Functions API course    Secrets and ordinary settings  Key Vault retrieval and App Configuration  No automatic rotation/live refresh claim    Inspect Function traces  KQL/log troubleshooting practice  No complete distributed OpenTelemetry instrumentation    
 Cosmos DB, Managed Redis, Container Apps/App Service specifics and broader monitoring work remain outside this workshop. Blob Storage and basic model calls support the application; their presence does not make every related service feature a measured exercise. 
 Cost drivers and cleanup 
 The four-hour US$5–15 planning allowance is intentionally approximate. It assumes one small node, a Burstable database, a few manuals, at most a handful of bounded eight-question demos, and prompt deletion. No bill has been measured for this implementation. Regional capacity, pricing agreements, minimum billing units and model token usage change the result. 
   Persistent until deletion:  AKS node/disks, database compute/storage, NAT/public IPs, ACR, Service Bus and App Configuration. Scaling the chat worker to zero does not remove these costs.   Usage-based:  model tokens, Function execution, storage operations/data transfer and log ingestion. Restrict repeated load runs; failed/retried model calls can also cost tokens.   After cleanup:  confirm ARM deletion and AKS's node-group removal. Soft-deleted Key Vault/App Configuration names remain subject to their recovery/retention behavior.  
 Use  Azure Pricing Calculator ,  AKS pricing ,  PostgreSQL pricing  and  Azure model pricing  before your own run. Budget alerts notify; they are not a hard spending cap. 
 Official documentation used
